chapter_summary:
Having grasped the fundamentals of blockchain and cryptography, we're now ready to understand how these technologies converge to form the vision of Web3. To truly appreciate Web3, it's helpful to look at the internet's evolution. The early internet, often called **Web1 (1990s-early 2000s)**, was primarily a "read-only" experience. Users consumed static content from websites, much like reading a digital newspaper. Interaction was minimal, and content creation was largely reserved for technical experts. Then came **Web2 (early 2000s-present)**, the "read-write" web. This era brought us social media, user-generated content, and interactive applications. Platforms like Facebook, Twitter, Google, and Amazon became dominant, offering incredible services and convenience. However, this convenience came at a cost: centralization. These platforms own your data, control access to your content, and act as intermediaries, creating "walled gardens" where they dictate terms, monetize your information, and can censor or de-platform users at will.

**Web3** emerges as the "read-write-own" web, a paradigm shift aiming to reclaim the internet's decentralized roots. It's built on the core principles of decentralization, user ownership, censorship resistance, and interoperability. In Web3, users own their data and digital assets, not the platforms. Instead of logging into a centralized service with a username and password, you interact with decentralized applications (dApps) using a cryptographic wallet (like MetaMask), which holds your private keys and represents your identity across the decentralized web. This shift empowers users by giving them direct control and a stake in the networks they participate in. No single entity can unilaterally decide to remove your content or freeze your assets; control is distributed across the network.

The foundation of Web3 is built upon several key technologies, with blockchain being the most prominent. Smart contracts, which are self-executing agreements stored on the blockchain, enable complex logic and automated interactions without intermediaries. Decentralized applications (dApps) are applications that run on a decentralized network, typically using smart contracts on a blockchain for their backend logic and data storage, with frontends often built using familiar web technologies like React (which we'll be using in this course). Other technologies like InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) provide decentralized storage solutions, ensuring that even static assets of dApps are not reliant on central servers. Web3.js is our primary tool in this course for connecting these React frontends to the blockchain, allowing our dApps to interact with smart contracts and user wallets.

Let's consider a practical example to highlight the difference between Web2 and Web3. Think about a social media platform. In **Web2** (e.g., Twitter), your profile, posts, and followers are all stored on Twitter's centralized servers. Twitter owns that data, can monetize it, and can block your account if they choose. In **Web3** (e.g., Lens Protocol, a decentralized social graph), your profile and posts might be stored on a blockchain or decentralized storage like IPFS, and linked to your cryptographic wallet. You own your social graph; if you decide to move to a different Web3 social frontend, you take your data and connections with you. The platform doesn't own your identity or content; you do. This fundamental difference extends to finance (DeFi vs. traditional banking), gaming (NFTs for in-game assets vs. centralized game items), and many other sectors.

While Web3 offers immense promise, it also faces challenges. Scalability (the ability to handle a large number of transactions quickly and cheaply) is a significant hurdle, though Layer 2 solutions are actively addressing this. User experience can be more complex than Web2, and regulatory landscapes are still evolving. Despite these challenges, the movement towards a more open, transparent, and user-owned internet is gaining momentum, and understanding Web3 is crucial for anyone looking to build the next generation of internet applications.

screens.title: Understanding Web3: The Decentralized Web
screens.subtitle: How blockchain, wallets, and decentralized storage reshape ownership, identity, and control on the internet.

narration.text: In this opening slide we set the stage for why Web3 matters. You will learn how the internet moved from a read-only set of static pages, to an interactive, platform-dominated web, and now toward a vision where users can genuinely own their digital identity and assets. We will make clear what changes under the hood: cryptographic wallets replace platform accounts, smart contracts automate agreement enforcement without intermediaries, and decentralized storage keeps content resilient and portable. A practical example you will revisit is social media: under Web2, a platform controls your profile and content; under Web3, your profile is tied to your wallet and can move with you. Along the way we'll highlight common confusions — for example, decentralization does not mean no rules; networks still have governance and trade-offs. By the end of this chapter you will be able to point to the core technologies that enable Web3, explain the read-write-own shift, and evaluate where Web3 is already practical and where it still faces limits like scalability and user experience. Keep in mind: understanding these building blocks helps you design dApps that respect user ownership and real-world constraints.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Web3 reframes the web as 'read-write-own' by combining blockchain, smart contracts, decentralized storage, and cryptographic wallets so users control identity and assets instead of centralized platforms.

screens.subtitle: What you will know and be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to trace how the web evolved from static pages to platforms that mediate interactions, and now toward networks that return ownership to users. First, you'll map Web1, Web2, and Web3 and describe the core differences including data ownership and identity. Second, you'll explain the defining principles of Web3: decentralization, user ownership, censorship resistance, and interoperability, and why each matters to real applications. Third, you'll identify the enabling technologies—blockchain, smart contracts, dApps, decentralized storage systems like IPFS, and cryptographic wallets—and describe their roles in a functioning dApp. Fourth, you'll compare Web2 and Web3 apps in a concrete way, using examples such as centralized social platforms versus decentralized social graphs, and discuss the trade-offs in scalability and user experience. These objectives prepare you to evaluate architecture choices and to build frontends that connect React applications to the blockchain using the right patterns.

screens.title: Evolution: Web1 → Web2 → Web3
screens.subtitle: A concise timeline showing how user roles and control changed over time

narration.text: Understanding Web3 begins with a clear timeline. In the 1990s, Web1 presented static pages where users mostly consumed content; publishing required technical skill and data lived on site owners' servers. With Web2, platforms democratized publishing and created read-write experiences — anyone could post, comment, and interact — but platforms centralized control, stored user data, and monetized it. Web3 proposes a third phase: read-write-own. Users still read and write, but they also hold ownership over digital assets and identity via cryptographic wallets. This change shifts where trust lives: rather than trusting a platform to hold and control data, users and decentralized networks enforce rules transparently. A common misconception is that Web3 simply moves everything to a blockchain; that's not accurate. Blockchains handle state and verifiable facts, smart contracts encode rules, and decentralized storage handles large content—each technology has a specific role. For designers, the takeaway is to choose the right layer for each requirement: store transaction-critical state on-chain, heavy media off-chain with decentralized storage, and let wallets manage identity and signing. Reflect: when would you prefer a centralized service despite possible loss of ownership?

keyIdea.title: Timeline insight
keyIdea.text: Web3 adds ownership to reading and writing, shifting trust from platforms to cryptographic proofs and distributed protocols; each technology plays a distinct role rather than a single monolithic change.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Evolution Timeline
Web1 → Web2 → Web3
Web1 — Read-only
Static pages and content publishing by site owners; users consume content and technical barriers limit who can publish.
Web2 — Read-write
Interactive platforms enable user-generated content and social features but centralize data and control in platform operators.
Web3 — Read-write-own
Users hold identity and assets via wallets; blockchains and decentralized storage provide shared, censorship-resistant primitives.
Why the layers matter
  • Blockchains store verifiable state and transactions, not large binary files.
  • Smart contracts automate rules without a trusted intermediary.
  • Decentralized storage holds heavy content while blockchains reference it via hashes.
Key takeaway
Treat Web3 as layered design: choose the correct layer for data, logic, and identity to avoid performance or cost mistakes.

screens.title: What Web3 Means: Read-Write-Own
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and how to apply it when designing applications

narration.text: Web3 is often summarized as read-write-own, but unpacking that phrase makes design decisions clearer. Read still means users view content and data. Write means users can create and modify content as in Web2. Own introduces a new requirement: the user must have control over identity and assets. In practice, ownership is represented by a cryptographic wallet which holds private keys that prove control of an address. This is not the same as a username and password; ownership is cryptographic and portable across applications. A common misconception is to equate ownership with absolute freedom: ownership gives control of assets, but networks still enforce protocol rules and often have governance. For example, a token you control can still be within a protocol that limits transfers via smart contract logic. When you design a dApp, ask: does this feature require verifiable ownership? If yes, the asset or reference should live in a format the user can control, such as a token or content hash linked to a wallet. That decision guides whether you store state on-chain, or keep it off-chain with references on the ledger.

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Treat 'own' as a requirement: if a user must prove control or move an asset between apps, use wallet-based ownership and persistent references rather than platform accounts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Read-Write-Own
Read • Write • Own
Define ownership as cryptographic control that can be demonstrated across dApps. Ownership changes how you design identity and data portability.
READ
Consume content like before.
WRITE
Create and interact live with apps.
OWN
Hold identity and assets via a wallet you control.
Concrete example
If a profile must move between different frontends, store a reference to the profile linked to a wallet address rather than keeping it locked in a platform account. This makes identity portable and under user control.
Common mistake
Putting large files directly on-chain because you think ownership requires on-chain storage. Instead, store content in decentralized storage and keep a hash on-chain.

screens.title: Cryptographic Wallets and Identity
screens.subtitle: How wallets represent identity and why they replace platform accounts in Web3

narration.text: A cryptographic wallet is the core identity mechanism in Web3. It stores private keys used to prove ownership and to sign transactions. When you connect to a dApp, you are not typically logging in with a username and password; you are authorizing the dApp to interact with an address you control. This model shifts responsibility: the user holds keys and thus control, while the dApp interacts with the user's wallet to request signatures or send transactions. An important distinction is between custody and ownership: if a wallet is custodial, a third party holds the keys on behalf of the user, which reintroduces centralization. A common misconception is that wallets store all user data; they primarily store keys and sign requests. Profile data or media may still live off-chain and be referenced by the blockchain. When designing UX, account for key management, recovery strategies, and the learning curve: wallet-based identity is powerful but requires helping users understand backup and private key safety. Consider whether custody or noncustody fits your users and the trade-offs that choice introduces. Cryptographic Wallets and Identity means wallets prove identity through key control; choose custody models and design recovery flows carefully to balance decentralization with usable ux.. In practical terms, how wallets represent identity and why they replace platform accounts in web3. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wallet takeaway
keyIdea.text: Wallets prove identity through key control; choose custody models and design recovery flows carefully to balance decentralization with usable UX.

Noncustodial
User holds private keys directly; maximum control and responsibility for backups.
Custodial

Concrete scenario

Pro tip
Clearly communicate recovery expectations. Users need simple guidance on seed phrase safety or custodial trade-offs to prevent account loss.

screens.title: Smart Contracts and dApps
screens.subtitle: How self-executing code and decentralized applications replace intermediaries

narration.text: Smart contracts are programs stored on a blockchain that run when triggered by transactions. They encode rules and enforce them without a central operator. Decentralized applications use smart contracts as their backend logic while providing a familiar web frontend for users. This allows features like token transfers, automated escrow, or rule-based access to run trustlessly. A concrete example: instead of a marketplace operator holding funds in escrow, a smart contract can hold funds and release them when both parties satisfy agreed conditions. A common misconception is that smart contracts are autonomous and flawless; in reality, they are code and must be carefully designed and audited, and their immutability can make bugs costly. When designing a dApp, separate on-chain and off-chain responsibilities: use smart contracts for verifiable, high-value state changes, and keep user interface state and large media off-chain. This hybrid approach preserves performance while leveraging trust guarantees where they matter most. Smart Contracts and dApps means use smart contracts for verifiable rules and settlement; keep heavy or ephemeral data off-chain and link it via references to control cost and scalability.. In practical terms, how self-executing code and decentralized applications replace intermediaries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contract design
keyIdea.text: Use smart contracts for verifiable rules and settlement; keep heavy or ephemeral data off-chain and link it via references to control cost and scalability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Smart Contracts & dApps
Smart contracts power dApp logic
They are self-executing rules on a blockchain that remove the need for trusted intermediaries for particular operations.
Example: escrow
A smart contract receives funds and releases them when both parties satisfy pre-defined conditions. No operator needs to intervene.
Design checklist
  • Put verifiable settlement and permission rules on-chain.
  • Keep large media and UI state off-chain and reference them from contracts.
  • Plan for audits and upgradeability to reduce immutability risk.
Common misconception
Believing smart contracts remove all governance. Smart contracts enforce rules, but governance mechanisms and network parameters still define how systems evolve.

screens.title: Decentralized Storage: IPFS and Content Hashing
screens.subtitle: Why large content is stored off-chain and how references keep it verifiable

narration.text: Blockchains are not efficient for storing large files, which is why decentralized storage systems like IPFS are essential to many dApps. IPFS stores content across a peer-to-peer network and addresses files by their hash, ensuring the content is verifiable: the hash changes if contents change. In practice, a dApp stores large media—images, videos, documents—on decentralized storage and places a reference hash on-chain. That hash becomes a permanent pointer that proves which content the contract intended to reference. A common mistake is to try to jam user media into on-chain storage because it seems simpler; this quickly becomes prohibitively expensive and reduces blockchain performance. When designing systems, treat the blockchain as the truth for small, critical state and proofs, and treat decentralized storage as the place for bulky, mutable media. Finally, ensure that you design for content availability: a reference is only useful if the content remains hosted by the network or pinning services. Decentralized Storage: IPFS and Content Hashing means store large or mutable content in decentralized storage and keep small, verifiable hashes on-chain for integrity and reference.. In practical terms, why large content is stored off-chain and how references keep it verifiable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Storage pattern
keyIdea.text: Store large or mutable content in decentralized storage and keep small, verifiable hashes on-chain for integrity and reference.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Decentralized Storage
IPFS and content hashing
IPFS stores content by hash. The blockchain stores hashes as proofs or references, not the heavy files themselves.
Concrete flow
Upload media to IPFS, receive a content hash, write that hash into a smart contract or metadata on-chain so that other dApps can verify the content's integrity.
Design checklist
  • Keep media off-chain; use IPFS or similar systems.
  • Store content hashes on-chain for verifiability.
  • Plan for pinning or hosting to ensure content availability.
Key takeaway
Use decentralized storage for files and the blockchain for proofs. This combination balances cost, performance and verifiability.

screens.title: Web2 vs Web3: Side-by-side Comparison
screens.subtitle: Login, data ownership, control, and portability contrasted

narration.text: A practical way to understand Web3 is to line up criteria and compare Web2 and Web3 approaches. In Web2 a user signs up with a username and password; a company stores profile data on their servers and controls access and monetization. In Web3, a user authorizes with a wallet; identity and ownership are tied to cryptographic keys and data is often referenced by hashes on-chain with main content stored in decentralized networks. This matters for portability: Web2 accounts are typically locked to a platform, while Web3 identity and assets can move between frontends. Another contrast is censorship and control: centralized platforms can remove accounts or content, whereas decentralized systems resist single-party takedowns—though governance and network rules still apply. A common misconception is that Web3 eliminates all friction; actually, wallet management, transaction costs, and network performance are new forms of friction. When choosing an architecture, weigh UX, trust model, and the need for true portability and censorship resistance versus the convenience and polish central platforms provide. Data ownership

Control & censorship

Portability

Practical question
Which trade-offs are acceptable for your users: the ease and polish of Web2, or the ownership and portability of Web3?

screens.title: Social Media: Web2 vs Web3 Example
screens.subtitle: A side-by-side look at a traditional social platform and a decentralized social graph

narration.text: Let's ground the ideas with a concrete social media example. In a Web2 social platform your profile, posts and social graph are stored on a platform's servers. The platform controls account creation, enforces moderation, and can monetize your data. In a decentralized social graph, profiles and posts are associated with wallet addresses and may be stored on-chain or on decentralized storage with on-chain references. This means you can switch frontends and retain your identity and connections. However, decentralization introduces design questions: how do you moderate harmful content without a central operator? How do you handle discovery of profiles when there is no single index? Also consider user onboarding: connecting a wallet replaces account creation but requires users to understand private keys and recovery. A clear misconception is that decentralization eliminates moderation needs; it does not — it changes where and how moderation and governance happen. The practical lesson is to design systems that combine portability with layers for moderation and indexing that respect users' ownership while keeping communities healthy. Concrete takeaway
Portability is powerful, but building a healthy social experience still requires thought about content moderation and user discovery that respects ownership.
Check your understanding

screens.title: How a dApp Interaction Typically Works
screens.subtitle: From wallet connection to on-chain state change — a practical sequence

narration.text: A common pattern in dApp interactions follows a clear sequence. First, the user connects their wallet to the frontend to establish identity. Next, the frontend prepares a transaction—this might be a request to call a smart contract function or to transfer a token. The dApp asks the wallet to sign or send the transaction; the wallet prompts the user to confirm. Once signed and broadcasted, the transaction is included in a block and the blockchain updates state. The frontend watches for confirmation and then updates its UI and any off-chain metadata references. A concrete example: a user posts content; the frontend uploads media to decentralized storage, receives a hash, then calls a smart contract to publish the reference. A misconception is thinking the frontend can force on-chain updates immediately; network confirmation times and fees affect when state is final. Good design surfaces pending states, explains fees, and makes signing explicit so users understand they are authorizing actions that affect ownership. screens.title: Core Technologies that Enable Web3
screens.subtitle: Blockchain, smart contracts, dApps, wallets, and decentralized storage in one stack

narration.text: Web3 uses a layered stack where each technology provides a distinct capability. The blockchain provides a shared ledger and consensus for verifiable state. Smart contracts live on that ledger to enforce application rules without intermediaries. dApps combine on-chain logic with web frontends to deliver user experiences. Wallets handle identity and authorization through cryptographic keys. Decentralized storage systems keep large files accessible and verifiable via content hashes placed on-chain. Understanding this architecture helps you place responsibilities correctly: use the blockchain where trust and verifiability matter, and use decentralized storage where size and cost require it. A typical misconception is thinking every piece must be decentralized; in many real applications, hybrid approaches that mix centralized APIs for performance with on-chain references for ownership are practical and acceptable. Finally, think about governance and upgrades: smart contracts and protocols often need mechanisms to evolve, and frontends will still provide the most polished user interactions. The practical effect is a system that combines guarantees with pragmatic engineering trade-offs. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Challenges Facing Web3
screens.subtitle: Scalability, user experience, and regulation — trade-offs to consider

narration.text: While Web3 promises ownership and decentralization, it also faces practical challenges you must plan for. Scalability is a core technical limit: blockchains can be slow and costly for high-volume interactions, which is why Layer 2 solutions and hybrid designs are common. User experience is another hurdle — wallet key management and transaction fees are unfamiliar to many users, so onboarding flows and clear messaging about signing and costs are essential. Regulatory uncertainty is a further constraint; laws around digital assets and data privacy can affect how you design custody, token models, and governance. A frequent misconception is that decentralization removes legal responsibility; in practice, developers and operators may still be subject to regulation depending on custody models and services provided. When building, weigh these trade-offs: use on-chain features only where they add measurable value like verifiability, use decentralized storage correctly, and plan user journeys that teach signing and backups. Ultimately, Web3 is evolving, and pragmatic hybrid architectures let you deliver useful experiences today while keeping future decentralization goals in sight. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Challenges
Scalability
Blockchains can be limited in throughput and cost; Layer 2 and off-chain patterns help but introduce complexity.
User experience
Users must manage keys and approve transactions; onboarding and recovery flows are critical design work.
Regulatory landscape
Legal rules around tokens, custody, and data can affect architecture and operations of dApps.
Misconception
Decentralization does not mean absence of governance or legal responsibility; it changes who enforces rules and how.
Actionable guidance
Prototype with hybrid approaches, prioritize clear UX for signing and recovery, and keep regulatory constraints in mind when choosing custody and token models.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important concepts to retain. First, Web1 was a read-only web of static pages, where publishing was controlled by site owners. Second, Web2 introduced read-write interactions and platforms that centralized data and control. Third, Web3 adds ownership: users hold identity and assets via cryptographic wallets, enabling portability and resistance to single-party censorship. Fourth, a decentralized application couples on-chain smart contracts with frontends and often uses decentralized storage for bulky content. These ideas form the vocabulary you'll use to evaluate system architecture and design choices. Keep these short definitions in mind as you build: they will help you decide what to put on-chain, what to keep off-chain, and how to design identity and recovery for real users. narration.text: Finally, keep these technology and principle reminders front and center. Smart contracts enforce rules without intermediaries but require careful design and audits. Decentralized storage systems let you store large content off-chain and keep hashes on-chain for verifiability. Wallets are the on-chain identity mechanism and determine custody models and recovery practices. And always weigh trade-offs: decentralization gives ownership and censorship resistance, but it introduces UX and scalability trade-offs that influence architecture. As you build, prioritize which guarantees you truly need on-chain and which you should implement off-chain with references. This pragmatic approach will let you deliver functional, user-friendly dApps today while preserving the core Web3 values of ownership and portability for the future.
